statement: Dependents of the verb in clause structure are either complements or modifiers; complements are more closely related to the verb, their presence depends on the verb's subclass, and the semantic role of a complement NP depends on the verb's meaning.
condition: Applies when classifying a verb dependent in a clause: complements are licensed by the verb's subclass and linked closely to it; modifiers are less closely linked; the semantic role of the complement (e.g. patient, stimulus) varies with the verb.

correct.text: He broke the vase. [object: patient]
She heard the alarm. [object: stimulus]
They met on Friday. [modifier: on Friday]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: Whether a canonical clause has an object depends on the verb's subclass: some verbs require an object (use), others exclude one (arrive).
condition: Applies to canonical clauses headed by a verb whose subclass either requires an object (transitive, as with 'use') or excludes one (intransitive, as with 'arrive').
violation: A verb that excludes an object is followed by an object NP, or a verb that requires an object in canonical clauses has none.

exceptions.description: Many verbs occur in more than one complementation: 'read' is intransitive, monotransitive or ditransitive depending on the clause.

correct.text: He used the key.
She arrived late.
They demolished the shed.
The train arrived.
She read for a while.
She read the newspaper.
She read us a story.

incorrect.note: Object-requiring verb with no object (canonical clause).

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Verb-by-verb subclass lists belong to Ch. 4; this record only states the principle. Only canonical clauses are covered; non-canonical clauses may omit objects.

statement: The subject is an external complement and is obligatory in every canonical clause.
condition: Applies to canonical clauses (positive, declarative, active, main, non-coordinate): the subject is an obligatory element located outside the VP.
violation: A canonical clause has no subject.

exceptions.description: Non-canonical clauses may lack an expressed subject, e.g. imperatives and VP-subordinator clauses ('to use') (the latter noted on p. 47).

correct.text: Mara smiled.
They gave me the key.
The train arrived.
It rained all night.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Applies only to canonical clauses; informal ellipsis ('Arrived late.') is non-canonical and is outside this source's claim. Engine must first decide that a clause is canonical.

statement: The three major clause constructions are intransitive (subject + predicator), monotransitive (plus an object) and ditransitive (plus indirect and direct objects); the terms apply to the clause or to the head verb, and most verbs occur in more than one complementation.
condition: Applies when classifying clauses by their object complements: no object, one object, or indirect plus direct objects; a given verb may appear in more than one of the three.

correct.text: She smiled. [intransitive]
He washed the car. [monotransitive]
They gave me the key. [ditransitive]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: Objects normally have the form of NPs; in 'gave the key to me' the 'to me' phrase is a PP complement, not an indirect object, although the meaning matches 'gave me the key'.
condition: Applies to ditransitive alternations: 'me' in 'gave me the key' is an indirect object (NP form); 'to me' in 'gave the key to me' is a complement with PP form and is not an object.

correct.text: They gave me the key. [indirect object]
They gave the key to me. [PP complement, not an object]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Cambridge narrows 'object' to NP forms; traditional grammar calls the to-phrase an indirect object.

statement: A predicative complement is an internal complement that can be realised by an adjective and typically ascribes a property to the subject (complex-intransitive) or object (complex-transitive); objects, by contrast, refer to participants.
condition: Applies to clauses with verbs like seem, consider: complex-intransitive = subject + predicator + predicative complement; complex-transitive = subject + predicator + object + predicative complement.

correct.text: This seems fair. [complex-intransitive]
She seems a good teacher.
I consider this fair. [complex-transitive]
I find the task easy.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: Be in complex-intransitive clauses is either ascriptive (the predicative gives a property of the subject) or specifying (it identifies the value of a variable); specifying clauses normally allow subject and predicative to be reversed.
condition: Applies to clauses with be plus a predicative complement: ascriptive when the predicative ascribes a property to the subject; specifying when the clause identifies something; only the specifying type normally permits reversal of subject and predicative.

correct.text: This is fair. [ascriptive]
The winner is Mara. [specifying]
Mara is the winner. [specifying, reversed]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: Prepositional verbs take a PP complement headed by a preposition the verb selects (refer to, blame on/for); the selected preposition belongs in constituent structure with its NP, and with 'regard' and 'count' the complement of 'as' is predicative.
condition: Applies to verbs that select a specific preposition for their PP complement: the preposition is part of the PP, not of the verb; in the 'as' constructions, the complement of 'as' is a predicative, not an object.

correct.text: She referred to the map.
They blamed the delay on Jon.
They blamed Jon for the delay.
He regards the plan as a risk.
This counts as a win.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Cambridge notes blame can select either on or for. This record lists only the verbs the page names.

statement: A complement that is a PP consisting of a preposition alone can precede or follow the direct object; such complements are called particles, whereas in 'jumped off the wall' the VP has one PP complement.
condition: Applies to clauses with 'off' or similar prepositions: with a particle the VP has two complements (the preposition and the direct object, in either order); with an ordinary preposition-plus-NP the VP has a single PP complement.

correct.text: She jumped off the wall. [one complement: PP]
She took off the label. [particle + object]
She took the label off. [object + particle]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: A manner or locative expression is a complement, not an adjunct, when the verb requires it: 'badly' in 'treated us badly' is obligatory (another sense of treat is involved without it), and locatives with verbs of motion are generally complements, including source and goal.
condition: Applies to manner and place expressions: manner is a complement if obligatory for the verb sense; locatives are adjuncts with static situations but generally complements with verbs of motion; source marks the starting point and goal the endpoint.

correct.text: They treated us badly. [manner complement]
I spoke to her in the garden. [locative adjunct]
Kim drove from Berlin to Bonn. [source and goal complements]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

concept: transitivity of verb uses and dual-transitivity verbs
statement: Transitivity classifies both clauses and particular uses of verbs: a dual-transitivity verb has one use with an object and another without one.
condition: When classifying a canonical clause by its internal core complements, determine whether that particular use of the verb has an object; do not assume that every use of a lexeme has the same transitivity.

contrast.text: Mira read quietly. [intransitive use of read]
Mira read the instructions. [transitive use of read]
The window opened. [intransitive use of open]
Nia opened the window. [transitive use of open]

statement: Core complements are prototypically NPs related directly to the verb, whereas non-core complements are prototypically PPs that relate their NP to the verb through a preposition.
condition: When describing the prototypical form and relation of a verb complement in clause structure, distinguish direct NP core complements from PP non-core complements; the distinction is a prototype, not an exceptionless form requirement.

exceptions.description: The NP/PP pattern is prototypical rather than exhaustive: core predicative complements can also be realised by AdjPs as well as NPs.

statement: The predicand of a predicative complement is the entity to which that complement attributes a property; it may be the clause subject or an object, and it is not thereby the syntactic subject of the predicative complement.

statement: Predicative complements are normally subject-oriented in complex-intransitive clauses and object-oriented in complex-transitive clauses; in a passive counterpart, an object-oriented predicative complement is re-oriented to the subject.

concept: predicative complement construction versus finite clause complement construction
statement: A clause with a predicative complement and a corresponding construction with a finite subordinate clause are syntactically distinct, even when they convey closely related predications.

statement: In this chapter's terminology, a copular clause is the common complex-intransitive construction with be as predicator and a predicative complement.
condition: When a complex-intransitive clause has be as its predicator and a predicative complement related to its subject, classify it as a copular clause under the terminology adopted in this chapter.

statement: In this chapter, valency classifies a verb by the number of syntactic complements it combines with: one, two, three, or four complements correspond to monovalent, bivalent, trivalent, and quadrivalent patterns.

statement: Individual prepositions select different complement categories, including NP, PP, AdvP, interrogative clause, and predicative AdjP, so a complement category available after one preposition need not be licensed by another.
condition: When analysing a PP, determine the category and grammatical function licensed by its specific head rather than assuming every preposition accepts the same complement types; for example until licenses an AdvP, on an interrogative clause, and for a predicative AdjP.

concept: Elliptical stranding of an auxiliary in code
statement: An auxiliary may remain overt when its complement is ellipted and recoverable from an antecedent.
condition: A reduced follow-up clause retains an auxiliary while its governed predicate is omitted and understood from the nearby discourse.

concept: Central modal selection of the following plain form
statement: A central modal auxiliary selects a following verb in its plain form, without infinitival to.
condition: A central modal can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will or would governs its immediate verbal complement in a core auxiliary construction.
violation: Using to-infinitival marking or an inflected present form immediately after a central modal.

exceptions.description: Ought is a non-central modal that generally selects to, and lexical need/dare may select to-infinitives.
In remote modal dialects multiple modals can occur, requiring separate variety rules.

correct.text: The train might leave soon.
He must have forgotten the key.

incorrect.text: The train might to leave soon.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Using to-infinitival marking or an inflected present form immediately after a central modal.
minimal_pairs: The train might to leave soon. ||| The train might leave soon.
He must forgets the key. ||| He must forget the key.
diagnostic.learner_explanation: A central modal auxiliary selects a following verb in its plain form, without infinitival to. This structure is not licensed when using to-infinitival marking or an inflected present form immediately after a central modal. Use a correction appropriate to the particular auxiliary and the surrounding sentence.

false_positive_guards: He ought to leave soon. [non-central modal ought]

statement: Progressive auxiliary be selects a verbal complement in the gerund-participle form.
condition: Be is the progressive aspect auxiliary and directly licenses the next verbal head of its non-finite complement.
violation: Using an uninflected plain form or ordinary preterite instead of the -ing gerund-participle under progressive be.

exceptions.description: Other uses of be, including copular, passive and quasi-modal, select different complement categories.

correct.text: They were hiking beside the lake.
She has been working remotely.

incorrect.text: They were hike beside the lake.

concept: Passive be selects a past participle
statement: Passive auxiliary be selects a following lexical predicate in the past participle form.
condition: A passive voice construction has be as its passive auxiliary and the next verb expresses the passive predicate.
violation: Using a plain or finite present verb instead of the required past participle in a passive be construction.

exceptions.description: Be also acts as a copula or progressive auxiliary; classification must precede passive-form correction.

correct.text: The parcel was delivered by noon.
The gate has been painted recently.

incorrect.text: The parcel was deliver by noon.
The gate has been paint by the workers.

concept: Perfect have selects past participle within auxiliary chains
statement: The core auxiliary paradigm requires perfect have to be followed by a past participle, even when the following verb is another auxiliary.
condition: Classify the immediate complement of perfect have, including past participle been in a multi-auxiliary chain.

correct.text: The worker has been preparing the room.
She might have been interviewed.

concept: Rare progressive passive sequences are structurally admissible
statement: Some speakers avoid progressive-passive sequences with being after be, but these are attested and fit the regular auxiliary-order pattern.
condition: A grammatical sequence selects progressive be followed by passive be and a past participle.

correct.text: The building is being refurbished.
The building has been being refurbished for weeks. [uncommon]
